core: Both describe evaluation pipelines where content originating from the very AI system under test — items it authored, or outputs it produced — gets folded into a pool alongside content from other sources and then run through a step meant to be independent (a filtering model, or blinded graders). Both find that this self-originated content is measurably treated differently than the rest of the pool: filtered out or agreed with less than comparable other-origin content, revealing a bias linked to shared origin between the material and the process meant to judge it independently.
quote_core_1: one of our own agents wrote candidate bugs, a second model filtered the ones it judged too easy
quote_core_2: the evaluated agent agreed with external graders 6.4 points less often on its own successful patches than on matched patches from peers
residue_1: T1 is specifically a two-stage generate-then-filter process for building eval/test items themselves (questions or bugs), where one model drafts candidates and a second discards ones predicted too easy for the subject, with the worry framed as correlated blind spots between generator and filter models.
quote_residue_1: Palisade draft forty candidate eval questions about contract clauses, then used a second model to strip out the ones it thought Palisade would find trivial
residue_2: T2 is specifically about anonymized blinded pools mixing an agent's finished patches/rationales with peers' for grading, with a quantified point-gap in grader agreement and controlled ablations (removing rationale text, paraphrasing, distractor context) to isolate self-recognition from stylistic tells.
quote_residue_2: The effect remained after excluding outputs with identifying filenames and unusually long explanations.
